Malaya invasion convoy, Force K-style convoy attacks, convoy escort, Malta resupply, commando fire support and a speculative nuclear successor.

segments.summary: A hypothetical force of fifteen to twenty improved X1-type submarines could attack German supply ships and Axis convoys, provided its deployment preserved the boats for suitable missions.
segments.question: How would fifteen to twenty improved X1 cruiser submarines change Britain's Second World War?
segments.answerShort: Improved successors could add long-range raider hunting, convoy attack, resupply and commando support. Their value would depend on reliable machinery and deployment, with disagreement over the risks and opportunities in the Mediterranean.

segments.title: The oldest warship still in active naval use
segments.body: A Brazilian river monitor is suggested as the oldest ship still actively used by a navy, although its name is recalled uncertainly. A Russian floating dock is also raised, with uncertainty over its damaged condition. The exchange does not settle a precise identification or a verified comparison.

evidence.note: Uncertain recollection of a Brazilian monitor's name and a damaged Russian floating dock, without a settled comparison.

segments.summary: A Brazilian river monitor and a Russian floating dock are suggested, with uncertainty over the name and condition of the vessels.
segments.question: What is the oldest ship still in service and actively used by a navy?
segments.answerShort: A Brazilian river monitor is the suggested answer, but its name is not settled. A Russian floating dock is also mentioned, with doubts about its condition.

segments.title: Who gets the blame for the Mark 14 torpedo?
segments.body: Most of the Bureau of Ordnance is the target of this angry, joking answer about who should have been replaced. King and Mush Morton are imagined confronting its personnel, with Nimitz cheering them on. The exchange assigns institutional blame without identifying particular officials or explaining the torpedo's defects.

evidence.note: Bureau of Ordnance blamed in a joking confrontation involving King, Mush Morton and Nimitz, without a technical account of the defects.

segments.summary: The Bureau of Ordnance receives the blame in a joking proposal to bring its personnel face to face with King and submarine commander Mush Morton.
segments.question: Who needed to be replaced to get the Mark 14 torpedo working early in the Second World War?
segments.answerShort: Most of the Bureau of Ordnance is blamed, with King and Mush Morton invoked as imagined sources of pressure. No specific replacement list is given.

segments.title: Designing a gun-based modern air-defense destroyer
segments.body: Daring's rapid-firing twin 4.5-inch mounts are the initial preference, with an enlarged ship carrying four twin mounts suggested. Clarifying that the ship is for the modern era changes the proposal to Italian automatic guns. One proposed battery has at least two larger guns for greater reach and at least six 3-inch mounts, ideally eight to ten, with six able to bear on a broadside. Close-in weapon systems would fill the remaining available capacity. The emphasis is on rate of fire and broadside coverage rather than a fully worked-out hull design.

evidence.note: Initial four-twin 4.5-inch Daring-derived proposal, then Italian automatic guns, six to ten 3-inch mounts and dense close-in armament for a modern ship.

segments.summary: Daring's twin 4.5-inch mounts are the historical starting point; a modern interpretation shifts to numerous Italian automatic guns and close-in weapons.
segments.question: What would the ultimate gun-based anti-aircraft destroyer look like?
segments.answerShort: The modern proposal combines larger guns for reach, numerous rapid-firing 3-inch mounts with strong broadside coverage, and as many effective close-in systems as the ship can accommodate.

segments.title: Richard I's Crusade fleet of cogs
segments.body: The question's Richard III is corrected to Richard I. His Crusade fleet is described as containing many cogs, with poor performance in storms singled out as a weakness. A brief aside recalls his sister's marriage to the king of Sicily and her less friendly treatment after his death.

evidence.note: Richard III corrected to Richard I, many cogs identified, a Sicilian family aside, and poor storm performance.

segments.summary: Many cogs carried Richard I's Crusade fleet, with poor performance in storms singled out as a weakness.
segments.question: What kind of fleet did Richard I take on Crusade?
segments.answerShort: Many cogs, with poor performance in storms.

segments.title: Can Britain sustain a competitive naval-shipyard model?
segments.body: Maintained naval shipyards with builders bidding for work receive a qualified endorsement. Economic viability depends on having enough work passing through the yards. The proposal therefore requires sufficient orders to sustain the arrangement.

evidence.note: Qualified support for maintained naval yards and bidding, with viability dependent on sufficient work.

segments.summary: A return to maintained naval yards with competitive bidding receives support, conditional on enough work to make the system viable.
segments.question: Should Britain maintain naval shipyards while builders bid competitively for the work?
segments.answerShort: Yes, provided there is enough work to make the arrangement economically viable.

segments.title: How early 2,000-horsepower engines would shape carriers
segments.body: More powerful piston engines or basic jets in 1935 would leave carrier designs broadly recognizable, with treaty arrangements still affecting what could be built. Britain would probably seek Implacable-like ships earlier. Aircraft power alone would not resolve the problem behind British armoured-carrier design: detecting incoming attacks far enough away to rely on fighters for protection. Until radar provided dependable warning, the carrier would still need to be designed to take a hit. The strategic comparison places American and Japanese operations in their Pacific backyard, while Britain faces operations on the other side of the world. A further argument expects a British approach through the South China Sea against Japanese trade, questioning how attractive that scenario would be to planners seeking larger battleships.

evidence.note: Treaty constraints, earlier Implacable-like designs, limited radar warning and carriers designed to take hits.
Different Pacific strategic settings and an argument that Britain would approach through the South China Sea against Japanese trade.

segments.summary: More powerful aircraft in 1935 would leave warning time, treaties and the ability to absorb hits central to British carrier design.
segments.question: What carriers would interwar navies build if 2,000-horsepower aircraft engines or basic jets existed in 1935?
segments.answerShort: Carrier designs would remain broadly familiar, with Britain probably seeking an Implacable-like design earlier. More powerful aircraft would not remove the need for protection while long-range warning remained uncertain.

segments.title: Thread forms and surface finishes in electrical fittings
segments.body: Run-on, identifying himself as a Virginia master electrician, describes problems with substitute fittings supplied for rooftop units. A nipple is a short pipe connecting fittings or boxes. His examples distinguish tapered threads from straight-cut threads and smooth internal surfaces from seams or sharp edges that could damage conductors. He also compares galvanized electrical fittings with the untreated material used in the substitute parts. In his account, extending the threads on replacement fittings without tapered threading dies spoiled the replacements as well. The practical issue is whether a readily available substitute retains the features needed for its intended application.

evidence.note: Run-on's professional identity and account of thread shape, seams, edges and material differences in electrical fittings.
Reported burrs and replacement fittings spoiled by rethreading without tapered dies.

segments.summary: Thread shape, internal seams and sharp edges matter when substitute pipe fittings carry electrical conductors.

segments.title: Professional responsibility for electrical installation quality
segments.body: Run-on replies that his colleagues either do not know or do not care about correct tap-and-die use. He connects his electrical qualification with a refusal to install work he considers wrong. He describes recommending larger conduit because the additional parts cost would be small compared with the labour involved. His concern includes a possible short destroying a control board costing $10,000 or more. That failure remains hypothetical, while his concern about being held responsible explains his willingness to accept an insubordination warning. He says that after speaking with the project manager, his foreman began leaving him alone.

evidence.note: Run-on's response to a tap-and-die question, conduit-sizing objection and professional qualification.
Hypothetical control-board failure, personal responsibility and Run-on's reported conversation with the project manager.

segments.summary: Conduit sizing and an imagined control-board failure illustrate the tension between supervisory instructions and an electrician's professional judgment.
segments.question: Did the crew know how to use a tap and die set correctly?
segments.answerShort: Run-on's view is that they either do not know or do not care. A dispute over conduit size illustrates his wider concern about following instructions he considers technically wrong.

segments.title: Photographic records and uncertainty about completed wiring
segments.body: Run-on keeps timestamped photographs of his work, particularly where the finished installation will be difficult to reach. He describes being told that polarity had been reversed on components in a 24-volt system, although he could not reconcile that report with his photographs. He acknowledges that he could be misinterpreting the images or could have made a later mistake, alongside the possibility that somebody else changed the work. His admission of previous mistakes gives the photographs a role in checking his own work as well as recording its completed condition.

evidence.note: Run-on's account of timestamped photographic records.
Unresolved polarity discrepancy, admitted alternative explanations and photographs of hard-to-reach installations.

segments.summary: Timestamped photographs preserve the condition of completed wiring and help examine disputed reports of later faults.
